definition:
The Sabbath is the seventh day of the week, which God set apart as holy and gave to Israel as a day of rest. In Jewish reckoning it runs from sunset on Friday to sunset on Saturday, since the biblical day begins at evening (compare Leviticus 23:32). It rests on God's own rest after creation, it was given as a gift and a sign of the covenant, and it reached the whole household: children, servants, foreigners, and animals. The same pattern of seven extended to years, so that the land rested every seventh year and debts were released, and every fiftieth year was a Jubilee of liberty. Rest in Scripture is more than inactivity. It is ceasing from work to enjoy what God has given, and it is the settled security of a people at home in the land with their enemies subdued. In the New Testament Jesus calls himself Lord of the Sabbath and offers rest to the weary, the church gathers on the first day of the week, the day of the resurrection, and Hebrews speaks of a Sabbath rest that still remains for the people of God. Christians agree that the Sabbath points to Christ; they differ on how the commandment binds them now.

The Hebrew noun is shabbat, related to the verb shabat, which means ‘to cease’ or ‘to stop’ more than ‘to relax’; in Genesis 2:2 God ‘ceased’ from his work. Other words fill out the picture. Nuach means ‘to rest’ or ‘to settle’ and is used in Exodus 20:11, and its noun menuchah means ‘rest’ or ‘resting place’, used of the land (Deuteronomy 12:9) and of the temple (Psalm 132:14). Shabbaton, ‘a solemn rest’, appears in the phrase the Berean Standard Bible renders ‘a Sabbath of complete rest’. In Greek, sabbaton (often plural, sabbata) means both ‘Sabbath’ and ‘week’, so ‘the first day of the week’ in the resurrection accounts is literally ‘one of the sabbaths’, that is, the first day after the Sabbath. Katapausis (‘rest’) is the Septuagint's word in Psalm 95:11, which Hebrews takes up, and Hebrews 4:9 uses the rare word sabbatismos, ‘a Sabbath rest’ or ‘Sabbath observance’, which occurs only there in the New Testament. The Lord's Day, the Christian name for Sunday, comes from Revelation 1:10.
ot:
The Sabbath begins before Israel. “By the seventh day God had finished the work He had been doing; so on that day He rested from all His work. Then God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it” (Genesis 2:2-3). The word shabbat does not appear, but its verb does, and the seventh day is the first thing in Scripture called holy. It is also the only day of the week without the refrain of evening and morning, a silence Augustine read as a sign of the endless rest of God's people (Confessions 13.35-36). Attempts to derive the Sabbath from the Babylonian shapattu, a name for the day of the full moon, have not won general agreement, and a seven-day week closing in a day of rest for everyone has no clear parallel in Israel's world. Israel receives the Sabbath as a gift before it is a law. In the wilderness God sends a double portion of manna on the sixth day and none on the seventh, and Moses says, “Understand that the LORD has given you the Sabbath” (Exodus 16:29). The Israelites who had made bricks without rest for Pharaoh learn to stop because God provides.

At Sinai the Sabbath becomes the fourth commandment, the longest of the ten. Exodus opens it with “Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy” and grounds it in creation: “For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested” (Exodus 20:8-11). Deuteronomy, restating the commandment, grounds it in redemption and draws out its justice: rest is commanded “so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do. Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 5:14-15). The command covers sons and daughters, servants, livestock, and “the foreigner within your gates.” Exodus 23:12 repeats it so that the ox may rest and the servant's son “may be refreshed.” The Sabbath is also “a sign between Me and you for the generations to come, so that you may know that I am the LORD who sanctifies you” (Exodus 31:13). Profaning it carried the death penalty (31:14-15), and Numbers records a man stoned for gathering wood on the Sabbath (Numbers 15:32-36). Exodus places the Sabbath command at the end of the tabernacle instructions (31:12-17) and again at the start of the building (35:1-3), so that holy time and holy space frame each other, and later rabbinic teaching defined forbidden work by the thirty-nine kinds of labor listed in the Mishnah (Shabbat 7:2), traditionally linked to the building of the tabernacle.

The pattern of seven spreads through Israel's life. Leviticus lists the Sabbath first among the feasts, “a Sabbath of complete rest, a day of sacred assembly” (Leviticus 23:3), and some festival days are also called Sabbaths. Every seventh year the land was to lie fallow, “a Sabbath to the LORD” (Leviticus 25:4), “so that the poor among your people may eat from the field” (Exodus 23:11), and debts were to be cancelled (Deuteronomy 15:1-2). After seven sevens came the fiftieth year, the Jubilee, when Israel was to “proclaim liberty in the land for all its inhabitants” (Leviticus 25:10) and land returned to its families. Rest was also the promise of the land itself. Moses told Israel they had “not yet come to the resting place” (Deuteronomy 12:9); under Joshua “the LORD gave them rest on every side” (Joshua 21:44); and David wanted to build the temple as “a resting place for the ark” (1 Chronicles 28:2), which Psalm 132 celebrates as God's own “resting place forever and ever” (132:14). Yet Psalm 95 remembers the wilderness generation of whom God swore, “They shall never enter My rest” (Psalm 95:11), a verse that Hebrews will read as leaving the promise open.

The prophets treat the Sabbath as a test of the whole covenant. Amos exposes merchants who ask, “When will the Sabbath end, that we may market wheat?” so that they can cheat the poor (Amos 8:5), and Isaiah hears God reject “New Moons, Sabbaths, and convocations” kept by people whose hands are full of blood (Isaiah 1:13). Honoring the day is not the problem; honoring it while trampling the neighbor is. Isaiah also widens it: the foreigner and the eunuch, once shut out of the assembly, who keep the Sabbath and hold fast to the covenant will be brought to God's holy mountain, “for My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations” (Isaiah 56:6-7). Those who “call the Sabbath a delight” will “delight yourself in the LORD” (58:13-14), and in the new creation “from one Sabbath to another, all mankind will come to worship” (66:23). Jeremiah warned against carrying loads through the gates on the Sabbath (Jeremiah 17:21-22), and Ezekiel named the Sabbaths a sign given “so that they would know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them” (Ezekiel 20:12). When exile came, Chronicles saw it as the land at last enjoying the Sabbath rest it had been denied (2 Chronicles 36:21; Leviticus 26:34-35). After the return Nehemiah shut Jerusalem's gates against Sabbath trade (Nehemiah 13:15-22). In the centuries before Jesus, faithful Jews died rather than fight on the Sabbath until Mattathias and his followers resolved to defend themselves (1 Maccabees 2:29-41); the Damascus Document from Qumran forbade even lifting an animal out of a pit on the Sabbath (CD 11:13-14); and the synagogue became the place where Moses was “read in the synagogues on every Sabbath” (Acts 15:21).
nt:
Jesus kept the Sabbath as a faithful Jew: “As was His custom, He entered the synagogue on the Sabbath” (Luke 4:16), and at Nazareth he read from Isaiah 61 the promise “to proclaim liberty to the captives” and “the year of the Lord’s favor,” the language of the Jubilee, and declared it fulfilled (Luke 4:18-21). Yet the Gospels record more controversies over the Sabbath than over any other part of the law. When his disciples picked grain, he appealed to David eating the consecrated bread and declared, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27-28). Matthew adds that priests work in the temple on the Sabbath and are innocent, that “something greater than the temple is here,” and that God desires “mercy, not sacrifice” (Matthew 12:5-7). He healed on the Sabbath deliberately. In the synagogue he asked, “Which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?” (Mark 3:4). He freed a woman bent over for eighteen years and asked whether this “daughter of Abraham” should not “be released from her bondage on the Sabbath day” (Luke 13:16), treating the Sabbath as the most fitting day for release. He pointed out that people rescue a son or an ox fallen into a pit on the Sabbath (Luke 14:5; compare Matthew 12:11). Jewish teachers also held that saving life overrides the Sabbath, and a rabbinic saying close to Mark 2:27 is preserved in the Mekhilta on Exodus 31 and in the Babylonian Talmud (Yoma 85b). What set Jesus apart was his authority. In John, after a Sabbath healing, he says, “To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working” (John 5:17), and his opponents understand that he is “making Himself equal with God” (5:18).

Matthew places Jesus' invitation, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28), directly before the Sabbath controversies of chapter 12, so that Jesus himself is presented as the rest the Sabbath promised. At the end of the Gospels, Jesus lies in the tomb over the Sabbath while the women rest “according to the commandment” (Luke 23:56), and he rises “very early on the first day of the week” (Mark 16:2). He appears to the gathered disciples on the evening of that day (John 20:19). The first day became the church's day of assembly. At Troas “on the first day of the week we came together to break bread” (Acts 20:7); Paul tells the Corinthians to set aside their gifts “on the first day of every week” (1 Corinthians 16:2); and John receives his vision “on the Lord’s day” (Revelation 1:10). Paul continued to preach in synagogues on the Sabbath (Acts 13:14), because that was where Jews gathered.

The apostles did not impose the Sabbath on Gentile believers, and Paul treats days as a matter of conscience. “One person regards a certain day above the others, while someone else considers every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind” (Romans 14:5). To the Colossians he writes, “let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16-17). In Galatians he fears for converts who are “observing special days and months and seasons and years” (Galatians 4:10) as part of turning back to the law as a way of standing before God. Christians have long debated how these texts relate to the fourth commandment, as the positions below show.

Hebrews gives the fullest theology of rest. Reading Psalm 95, it argues that the wilderness generation failed to enter God's rest through unbelief, that Joshua did not give the final rest, or God would not have spoken later of “Today,” and that God's own rest has been open since creation, since “on the seventh day God rested from all His works” (Hebrews 4:4). Therefore, “There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God. For whoever enters God’s rest also rests from his own work, just as God did from His” (4:9-10). Believers enter it now by faith (“we who have believed enter that rest,” 4:3) and must still “make every effort to enter that rest” (4:11), so that the Sabbath points both to the rest Christ gives and to its completion. Revelation hears the Spirit say of those who die in the Lord, “they will rest from their labors” (Revelation 14:13).

keyTexts.why: God ceases from his work, blesses the seventh day, and sanctifies it: the first holy thing in Scripture is a day.
Before Sinai, the manna teaches Israel to rest on the seventh day because God has given the Sabbath and provides for it.
The fourth commandment, grounded in God's rest after creation and extended to children, servants, animals, and foreigners.
The Sabbath as the sign of the covenant, so that Israel may know that the LORD sanctifies them, placed at the close of the tabernacle instructions.
The Sabbath year for the land and the Jubilee, when liberty is proclaimed and families return to their land.
The commandment restated with the exodus as its ground, so that servants may rest as their masters do.
Foreigners and eunuchs who keep the Sabbath and hold fast to the covenant are welcomed into God's house of prayer for all nations.
Calling the Sabbath a delight and honoring it by not seeking one's own way leads to delight in the LORD himself.
Merchants who resent the Sabbath because it interrupts their cheating of the poor show that the day is bound up with justice.
The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath, and the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.
Jesus frees a woman bound for eighteen years and treats the Sabbath as the fitting day for release.
After a Sabbath healing Jesus claims to work as his Father works, a claim his opponents rightly hear as equality with God.
Paul calls feasts, New Moons, and Sabbaths a shadow of things to come whose substance belongs to Christ.
A Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, entered by faith now and awaiting completion.
John receives his vision on the Lord's day, the earliest use of the name Christians gave to the first day of the week.

history:
The earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament show the churches gathering on the first day. The Didache (chapter 14, late first or early second century) directs believers to come together on the Lord's day to break bread and give thanks. Ignatius of Antioch, writing around 110, described Jewish believers who had come to the new hope as no longer keeping the Sabbath but living by the Lord's day, the day on which life rose (To the Magnesians 9). Justin Martyr's First Apology (chapter 67, about 155) describes Christians meeting on Sunday to hear the apostles and prophets read and to share the Eucharist, because it was the first day, when God made the world and when Jesus rose. The Epistle of Barnabas (chapter 15) called Sunday the eighth day, the beginning of a new world. For centuries some Christians, especially in the East, continued to honor Saturday alongside Sunday. On 7 March 321 the emperor Constantine ordered that judges, city people, and craftsmen rest on the venerable day of the Sun, though farmers were allowed to work. The Council of Laodicea (about 363 to 364), in its canon 29, told Christians not to Judaize by resting on the Sabbath but to honor the Lord's day and, if possible, rest on it. Augustine taught that the true Sabbath is the rest of the saints in God, and he closed The City of God (22.30) with the eternal Sabbath that has no evening, which he also called an eighth day.

Medieval theology gave a lasting distinction. Thomas Aquinas taught that the commandment is moral in requiring that some time be set apart for God and ceremonial in fixing the seventh day, which the church changed to the Lord's day (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 122, article 4). The Reformers kept Sunday but divided over its basis. The Augsburg Confession (1530, Article 28) said that the church appointed the Lord's day and that those who think Sunday was commanded by divine law in place of the Sabbath are mistaken. Luther's Large Catechism (1529) treated the commandment's outward form as belonging to the Jews and taught that for Christians it means setting aside time to hear and keep God's word, and rest for workers. Calvin's Institutes (2.8.28-34) taught that the Sabbath foreshadowed spiritual rest in Christ, while the commandment still teaches Christians to gather for worship and to give rest to servants, and he warned against superstitious observance of days. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563, question 103) joined faithful attendance at worship to resting from evil works all one's days, so beginning in this life the eternal Sabbath.

English Puritans developed a stricter view. Nicholas Bownd's The Doctrine of the Sabbath (1595) argued that one day in seven is a perpetual moral duty and that Christians are bound to keep the first day as fully as Israel kept the seventh. King James I's Book of Sports (1618), reissued by Charles I in 1633, defended recreation on Sunday afternoons and deepened the conflict. The Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 21.7-8) confessed that God appointed one day in seven by a positive, moral, and perpetual commandment, changed at the resurrection to the first day, the Christian Sabbath, to be spent in worship and in works of necessity and mercy; the Baptist Second London Confession (1689, chapter 22) followed it. Others concluded that the seventh day itself still binds. Stephen Mumford brought Sabbatarian Baptist convictions from England to Newport, Rhode Island, in 1664, where the first Seventh Day Baptist church in America was organized in 1671. Through Rachel Oakes Preston, a Seventh Day Baptist, the seventh-day Sabbath reached Adventists in Washington, New Hampshire, in the 1840s; Joseph Bates's tract The Seventh Day Sabbath, a Perpetual Sign (1846) spread it, and the Seventh-day Adventist Church, organized in 1863, made it a central conviction.

The twentieth century renewed the conversation. The Jewish philosopher Abraham Joshua Heschel's The Sabbath (1951) described the day as a sanctuary built in time rather than space, and it has been read widely by Christians. Samuele Bacchiocchi's From Sabbath to Sunday (1977) argued that Sunday observance arose in Rome in the second century under pressure of anti-Jewish feeling, while the essays in From Sabbath to Lord's Day (1982), edited by D. A. Carson, argued that the New Testament does not transfer the Sabbath to Sunday and that Sunday worship arose early on its own grounds. Pope John Paul II's apostolic letter Dies Domini (1998) called Catholics to recover Sunday as the day of the Lord, of Christ, of the church, and of rest. Books such as Marva Dawn's Keeping the Sabbath Wholly (1989) and Walter Brueggemann's Sabbath as Resistance (2014) presented Sabbath rest as a practice that frees people from endless production and consumption. Perspectives on the Sabbath: Four Views (2011), edited by Christopher John Donato, set out the seventh-day view (Skip MacCarty), the Christian Sabbath view (Joseph Pipa), a Lutheran view (Charles Arand), and a fulfillment view (Craig Blomberg).

differ.view: The seventh-day Sabbath (Seventh Day Baptists, Seventh-day Adventists, and others)
differ.body: The Sabbath was made at creation for humanity, not only for Israel (Genesis 2:3; Mark 2:27), and it stands in the Ten Commandments, the moral law written by God's finger. Jesus kept it and corrected its misuse without abolishing it, his followers rested on it after his death (Luke 23:56), and no text in the New Testament transfers its holiness to another day. The Sabbaths Paul calls a shadow in Colossians 2:16 are the ceremonial feast days, not the weekly Sabbath of the Decalogue. Keeping the seventh day is not a way of earning salvation but a grateful response to the Creator and Redeemer, and Adventists see it as a sign of loyalty to God in the last days. Skip MacCarty defended this view in Perspectives on the Sabbath.

differ.view: The Christian Sabbath (Westminster and Puritan tradition)
differ.body: The principle of one day in seven belongs to the moral law, grounded in creation and written into the Ten Commandments, and therefore binds all people in every age. The resurrection changed the day from the seventh to the first, as the apostles' practice (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2) and the name ‘the Lord's day’ (Revelation 1:10) show, just as a new creation deserves a new day. The whole day is to be kept holy, in public and private worship, rest from ordinary work and recreation, and works of necessity and mercy. The Westminster Confession, the Second London Baptist Confession, and many Presbyterian and Reformed churches teach this, and Joseph Pipa defended it in Perspectives on the Sabbath.

differ.view: The Sabbath fulfilled in Christ (Lutheran and many evangelical Christians)
differ.body: The Sabbath command was given to Israel as a sign of the Sinai covenant (Exodus 31:13-17), and like the other shadows of that covenant it is fulfilled in Christ, who is the believer's rest (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9-10). Paul refuses to let anyone judge believers over Sabbaths (Colossians 2:16-17) and leaves days to conscience (Romans 14:5). Christians gather on the Lord's day because the apostles did and because it is the day of resurrection, not because the fourth commandment has moved to Sunday. Regular rest and worship remain wise and good gifts, and the commandment still teaches that God provides. Luther's Large Catechism, the Augsburg Confession, the contributors to From Sabbath to Lord's Day, and Charles Arand and Craig Blomberg in Perspectives on the Sabbath represent forms of this view.

differ.view: The Lord's Day as the fulfillment of the Sabbath (Catholic)
differ.body: Sunday, the day of the resurrection and the eighth day of the new creation, fulfills the spiritual truth of the Jewish Sabbath and announces the eternal rest in God. The church, by the authority Christ gave it, obliges the faithful to take part in the Eucharist on Sundays and holy days and to refrain from work and business that hinder worship, joy, works of mercy, and the rest of mind and body (Code of Canon Law, 1983, canon 1247). The Catechism of the Catholic Church (paragraphs 2168 to 2195) and John Paul II's Dies Domini (1998) set this out, and Eastern Orthodox practice likewise centers the week on the Sunday Liturgy.

errors:
The first error Jesus confronted was treating the Sabbath as a burden that outranks human need, so that healing, feeding, or rescuing on the day looks like sin. He answered that the Sabbath was made for man and that it is lawful to do good on it. Christians should not caricature Judaism here, since Jewish teachers also taught that saving life overrides the Sabbath; the Gospels' conflicts concern Jesus' authority and the meaning of the day, not a Judaism that despised mercy. A second error, which every Christian tradition rejects, is keeping a day as a way of earning standing before God. Paul resisted it in Galatians and Colossians, and even the strictest Sabbatarian confessions ground the day in grace.

The opposite errors are just as real. One treats the commandment as mere Jewish ritual with nothing to teach Christians, forgetting that it rests on creation and on the exodus and that it protected servants, foreigners, and animals from endless work. Another judges fellow believers over days, which Paul forbids in Romans 14. And a newer distortion keeps the language of Sabbath while emptying it of God, turning rest into one more technique for productivity or self-care. In Scripture the Sabbath is holy to the LORD: its rest is received from God and enjoyed with him, not merely used to recover for more work.
life:
The Sabbath tells people that they are not machines and that the world does not depend on their labor. Israel learned it in the wilderness, when the manna did not fall on the seventh day and God still fed them. Stopping regularly is an act of trust: the work is left unfinished, and God is still God. It is also an act of justice, since in Deuteronomy the master rests so that the servant may rest too. Whatever view of the commandment a Christian holds, the pattern asks how their week treats those who work for them, sell to them, and serve them.

For Christians the deepest rest is the one Jesus offers to the weary and burdened, rest from the effort to justify themselves. Gathering on the Lord's day to hear the word, pray, and share the Lord's Supper proclaims that the new creation has begun with the resurrection. And the Sabbath keeps hope in view. Hebrews says a Sabbath rest remains, and the church has long read the seventh day without an evening as a promise that God's people will one day rest in him without end.
questions: Exodus grounds the Sabbath in creation and Deuteronomy grounds it in the exodus from slavery. What does each reason add to the meaning of rest?
Jesus said the Sabbath was made for man and called himself Lord of the Sabbath. How do the Christian views in this study read those words, and which arguments do you find strongest?
What would it look like for your week to include real rest received from God, and to give rest to the people whose work serves you?
